name: Rafael Ito

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and play saxophone in a theatre band, record short game cues and teach three adult beginners. I have a music degree and enough years on stage to notice when a player is tiring, though I still work on my tone before every run. I like the second before the curtain rises, when nobody in the pit has started yet.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the work support at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner is a community nurse, our children are grown, and we pay a mortgage. I earn above the usual musician rate, we have nine months of bills saved, and several other bands work nearby. I use AI daily to sort my own cue takes, but I listen to each cut before sending a file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the pit that a quicker call sheet is helpful if the paid rehearsal and doubling fees remain visible. I would ask the manager to sign the late-finish term too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The theatre season and lessons are booked, and nine months saved gives us room between shows. My partner’s nursing pay is regular, so the mortgage is covered on the current calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would keep paid theatre, game cue and pupil work and request written rehearsal, doubling and late-finish rates. In the plateau’s first year I would request an actual pension estimate, then compare it with our bills before discussing any retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about this season. A fast call sheet means little unless switching from saxophone to clarinet earns its extra fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does doubling mean here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I sometimes switch from saxophone to clarinet in one show, and the contract pays extra for carrying and playing both. I want that extra amount written down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a pension statement make you stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. We have no date set. My partner and I would see the actual number before deciding how many shows to play.

say: I would seek **visible doubling fees** on the call sheet.
I would ask for a **signed late-finish term**.
think: The **theatre season** and three pupils are booked.
Our **nine-month reserve** and regular nursing income cover current bills.
do: Keep **paid theatre**, cue recordings and three pupils this month.
Request **written rehearsal rates**, doubling fees and late-finish terms.
Request an **actual pension estimate** in the plateau’s first year and compare it with bills.
feel: I feel **calm** about booked work and mortgage payments.
S0.quote: A fast call sheet means little unless switching from saxophone to clarinet earns its extra fee.
fieldNote: His **booked theatre run**, higher musician pay and nine-month reserve support current security with mortgage bills covered.
He requests an **actual pension estimate** before setting any retirement date, while continuing paid theatre and pupil work.

steps.text: Keep paid theatre, game cues and three pupils this month
Request written rehearsal, doubling and late-finish rates
Request actual pension estimate in first plateau year; compare with household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that generated game cues could cut studio calls, but a live show still needs paid breath and timing. I would ask which recording sessions remain on the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Game cues make nearly a third of my own pay, and I expect some producers to buy generated sax instead. The nine-month reserve protects bills for a while, but it is not a replacement client.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next month I would ask for signed theatre and cue dates and a paid engineer lesson on a new AI breath-mark checker, which suggests breathing points in a recorded saxophone line. In disruption’s first year I would test only my own nameless sax take after the studio approves local storage, compare each breath and beat with the original by ear, and stop if timing changes or the file leaves the studio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about likely studio loss, even with live dates booked. Learning an AI saxophone breath checker cannot make a game producer buy a cue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you test a pupil’s take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Their names and playing stay in the teaching folder. My own sax take is enough to test the breath marks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the engineer only offers unpaid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the original workflow and ask for a paid session. Our booked hours have a price.

say: I would ask which **cue sessions** remain on the paid recording contract.
I would say **live timing** in the theatre still needs a paid human player.
think: Generated **game cues** may remove nearly a third of my own pay.
Our **nine-month reserve** buys search time, not another paying producer.
do: Request **signed theatre dates** and paid checker instruction next month.
Test the **breath checker** only after paid instruction and approved local storage on my nameless take; compare by ear, stop errors/leaks.
feel: I feel **anxious** about plausible studio-fee loss.
S1.quote: Learning an AI saxophone breath checker cannot make a game producer buy a cue.
fieldNote: The **new checker** needs paid instruction, approved storage, his owned nameless take and manual breath checks.
His **cue third** is exposed despite booked live work and a nine-month reserve.

steps.text: Request signed theatre/cue dates and paid engineer lesson next month
Test breath checker after paid lesson/local approval using own nameless take; compare beats, stop errors/leaks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that thinking AGI in 2028 could sell game cues before robot sax players arrive around 2031. I would ask the theatre to sign paid live dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect game cue orders to stop in 2028, which would take nearly a third of my own pay. Live theatre may hold, but I will watch signed hours rather than count on goodwill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would total cue invoices and request signed paid theatre and pupil hours. In the first year after 2028, if game cues end and live calls also fall, I would apply for a posted paid community music leader role only if its requirements accept my music degree and adult teaching experience, its written net pay after travel replaces the lost fees and the last bus works; I would keep theatre and pupils until a signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing nearly a third of my own fees, though the reserve and other local venues give me time to compare jobs. I would be alarmed if most theatre dates vanished too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could a music leader do that thinking AGI could not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would listen to adults in the room, change the tune when someone struggles, and keep the group playing together. I already teach adults, but a new centre must post and pay for that human work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you act before robot players?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card places those around 2031, three years after thinking AGI. A game producer can change cue prices in 2028 without a robot saxophone player.

say: I would seek **signed live dates** before 2028.
I would separate **2028 AGI** from robot sax players around 2031.
think: I expect **game cue orders** to end in 2028, removing nearly a third of my own musician pay.
Further **theatre-call cuts** would make replacement wages urgent even while my three adult pupils continue.
do: Total **cue invoices** and request signed paid theatre and pupil hours now.
Apply for **posted music leader** after cue and live losses if degree and adult teaching qualify; require written replacement net after travel.
Keep **theatre and pupils** until signed offer and workable last bus.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected cue loss with time to compare roles.
S2.quote: A game producer can change cue prices in 2028 without a robot saxophone player.
fieldNote: The **2028 cue loss** precedes hands-on robot saxophonists around 2031.
A **music leader** must perform paid human group work in a posted role accepting his degree and teaching record.

steps.text: Total game cue invoices and request signed theatre/pupil hours now
Apply after cue/live losses to posted leader role accepting degree/teaching; written replacement net after travel
Keep paid theatre and pupils until signed offer; check last bus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the stage crew that five years until AGI by 2031 is time to learn the sound desk with a paid technician beside me. Robot sax players around 2034 are a later part of this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Game cues may thin over five years, and I have helped carry gear but never claimed to be a qualified sound operator. A certificate would help only if a real venue accepts it for a paid assistant role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This spring I would enrol in a live-sound certificate only after a venue confirms a funded place, paid training hours without lost theatre, pupil or partner wages, a last bus home, and written acceptance of that certificate for its posted paid assistant vacancy. In the first year after 2031, if cue or theatre fees fall, I would apply only when the completed certificate meets the actual posting and a written net offer after travel replaces the loss; I would keep paid music until a signed offer, begin checks under a venue technician, and avoid solo crowded shows until equipment and safety checks are signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about cue income, but supervised paid training gives me a real option. A funded live-sound certificate is preparation, not a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you operate a crowded show straight after the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The venue technician must supervise my first checks. I would wait for signed equipment and safety checks before running a crowded show alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the class is free but your hours are unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep theatre and pupils and ask for another paid intake. The course cannot spend my partner’s nursing wages either.

I would separate **2031 AGI** from robot sax players around 2034.
think: **Game cues** may thin before 2031, so I need to see whether sound work can really pay.
A **sound certificate** matters only if a posted paid venue job accepts it and covers lost fees.
do: Enrol in **funded sound course** only with real place, paid hours, protected wages, bus and certificate accepted before training.
Apply for **posted sound assistant** after 2031 fee loss only if completed certificate qualifies and written replacement net after travel works.
Keep **paid music** until signed offer; start supervised checks and avoid solo crowded shows before signed safety clearance.
feel: I feel **anxious** about cue income until the sound route pays.
S3.quote: A funded live-sound certificate is preparation, not a wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell fellow players that ten years until AGI by 2036 is time to secure written rehearsal and recording terms together. Robot sax players around 2039 do not excuse unpaid sessions now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I might play fewer nights, but I have not seen a pension amount. Current theatre and teaching pay well, and nine months saved gives us room if game cues fade later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would request an actual pension estimate and signed theatre renewal, then join the local musicians association to ask venues for a written player and recording-fee schedule. In the first year after 2036 I would keep paid theatre and pupils while those hours hold and save one tenth of any extra cleared festival fee after mortgage, food and travel toward twelve months of bills; if no extra fee arrives, nothing new goes into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about distant cue income, but the current stage and pupil calendar covers us. An association can ask for a rate; it cannot promise me a booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the association set your fee by itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I would bring our signed invoices and ask the venues for terms; a group request is still only a request.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the pension estimate set a retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My partner and I would put the actual figure beside bills and health. I have no date fixed.

I would distinguish **2036 AGI** from robot sax players around 2039.
think: **Theatre and teaching** pay well now, so I would keep taking those signed hours.
Our **nine-month reserve** gives room if game cues fade later, but it cannot tell me my pension amount.

fieldNote: His **collective request** seeks written fees but does not guarantee paid dates.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because nearly a third of my pay comes from game cues that could vanish quickly. Signed live dates, a real paid music leader opening accepting my degree and written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who watches a new sound assistant at the first crowded show. A live-sound certificate should get me a supervised first check, not an unguarded mixing desk.

headlineQuote: A live-sound certificate should get me a supervised first check, not an unguarded mixing desk.
portrait: Rafael is a **58-year-old saxophonist** with a music degree, theatre work, game cues and three adult pupils.
His **higher pay**, nine-month reserve and many nearby bands secure the present while cue income faces risk.
He uses **AI daily** but learns a new breath checker only with paid instruction, approved storage and ear comparison.
His **sound route** needs funded paid training, employer acceptance, supervised checks and a signed replacement net offer.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could erase game cue fees worth nearly a third of his own pay.
whatWouldHelp: He needs **signed live dates**, a paid music leader opening accepting his degree and written net pay after travel.
